NEW BOOKS.

How The Claims Of The Season Love and Lucy. By Maurice Hewlett. London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd. Are To Be Met. It comes as a surprise to find that Mr. Hewlett is writing about modern every-day life—the life of the West End of London to-day, with its clubs, parks. motors and telephones, and all the other things comprised in our modern civilisation. Mr. Hewlett is . accus- tomed, to write of more primitive times and people He has laid us undet a debt of obliga- tion by his charming stories of Italy, and one

The activities of the people always having in- cluded shopping at Christmas time, they are sure to be repeated this -year in almost as in- tense a measure as usual. Against Warrington it could not be contended that the majority of its citizens were wasteful and extravagant, and a sensation-monger would not-have the material upon which to condemn us as he had when he visited Manchester, Liverpool, and other large places. No, Warrington A just right. It is level-headed with its purse. To us Christmastide is a season for replenish- ment. The shopkeepers 'know that, and have made their establishments attractive with wholesome, useful and ornamental goods. A walk along the main thoroughfares is interest- ing as of yore. Of course, much of the many- coloured frills of the past have gone, and those who love the garish in spite of tears are dis- appointed. But the subdued tone is in keeping with great events, and display's have losenoth- ing in effectiveness. The loudness has been _quieted, and the goods of their own inherent beauty and usefulness make their appeal with- out gaudy surroundings. A tour of the shops brings one into direct contact with the spirit of the nation—cheerfulness, dignity, and utilitar- ianism.

may imagine that in this piesent -book his object was to show that the passions which sway men and: women are as much in force in London to-day as they were in Italy a few hundred years ago. The story centres mainly about three people—a highly respectable and successful solicitor, his charming wife, and the tertitmi quid, in this case a very forceful and overpowering personality. Some very unusual incidents occur in the course of the story, and the thlicitor and his wife also behave at times in an unexpected manner, but probably Mr. Hewlett is right in contending that, there are two natures in every one of us, and that. given the necessary circumstances, you will find the Londoner of to-day acting in the same way as the people described by the author in kis "little novels of, Italy." Mr. Hewlett has written an interesting book.. It will hardly take rank with his famous historical novels, but in Mrs. Macartney he ,has drawn a very fine and tender character, and .her husband also rises to heights of nobility which we should never have ex- pected of him.

The success of the Raynor Repertoire Com- pany is speaking for itself, kind I propose to devote all my space to next week's announee- ment. That wonderful and epoch-making spec- tacle in the opicture world "The Birth of a Nation," is due. It is a unique production. It is not an ordinary film; in fact, it has never been shown at a -pichire house, the promoters only allowing •it to be presented at the better- class theatres.

It is a production which unfolds the' thrilling romance of the war in America and the re-con- struction of the Southland, and In order that it may have a striking effect various appurten- ances are brought into requisition. As many as four lorries are required to convey "the effects," and an orchestra of 31 in number (it reminds one of grand opera) are to be em- ployed. "The Birth of a Nation" has enjoyed a run of four weeks in Liverpool and nine in Manchester.

' "The' Birth of a Nation" 'is the largest and most important, production of a decade, yet not a word is spoken throughout the performance of nearly three hours. Music supplies the absence of speech. Some idea of its magnitude may be had from the facts that 18,000 actors and 5,000 horses took part, and that the staging of this great " outdoor " drama cost £lOO,OOO. It took eight months to produce.
There is a trio of girls in "The Birth of a. Nation" whose combined salaries run up to con- siderably over 0E20,000 a year, and none are out of their teens.

Mr. Griffith understands the force of contrast in art as well as even', other detail of this fascinating, form Of expression whio he has made famous. In the three, youthful stars of his he has the satisfaction of- seeing his work car- ried out triumphantly by three girls Oho have been trained under his guiding direction. Mae Marsh is red-headed and clover far beyond the run of her eighteen. years.
Lillian Gish is pronounced the finest type of blonde in America. She has been in the profes- sion now for several years, beginning under Mr. Griffith's direction when a mere schoolgirl.

Miriam Cooper is the newest member of the trio, and has only been in the profession about a year now. She has come forward ,steadily, and her work in "The Birth e a I,..tation.",has enhanced her earning capacity. Miss Cooper is the Southern type. She is willowy and languid, and a pronounced •brunette, - ---------- Palace and Hippodrome.

Leading the bill this week is Cooper Mitchell, a racy story teller and entertainer at the piano. He has ("alto a host of good stories, and his original compositions have exceptional merit, dealing as they do with present-day topics. Wal Marsden, the Lan- cashire Lad, an old favourite, had a splendid reception. His songs and patter are 'extremely characteristic and the dialect tales and jokes go with a rare swing.

We might almost say that the Allies have united this week to entertain us in the Hippo- drome, as we have two famous Franco-Italian stars in the equilibristic World; a troupe of Japanese performers, and musical acrobatic comedians from Italy. The fvt-mentioned performers. the "Two Lillys,"7 are simply marvellous in their head-to-head 'balancing while doing a musical act as well; and the Royal TOkiwa Family, clad in gorgeous native raiment, accomplish most difficult and unique acrobatic feats, hill of humour. The Bene- detti Brothers, are an extremely funny pair, and the marvellous way in which they play violins and throw somersaults simultaneously has hover been excelled.

In the conjuring line Allan Shaw mystifies his audience by the 'facility: with. which he accumulates coins from ,the atmosphere—an extremely useful accomplishment nowadays. Harry Bradshaw, an excellent tenor, sings some fine songs; not of the hackneyed type, but thoroughly enjoyable.
The little special by the orchestra this week is a drum solo .by Mr. E. Higham, entitled "The Drummer's Birthday." It is well worth hearing.

A lady who tops the bill wherever she ;oes is due at the Palace and Hippodrome net reek. She is Miss May 'Henderson,: known- as 'The Dusky Comedy Queen," and is in the front -rank of comediennes. She is of the vigorous, b •uny and bright type, full of wif and laughter. The management are to be congratulated Upon their enterprise in "securing such a "star." Supply Scheme.
A MOTOR CAR TO HELP.

Is a big water supply scheme in contempla- tion in Warrington? At the Town Council meeting on Thesday Councillor Gough said he - noticed on the private agenda that at the last meeting of. the Water Committee "ft" report by Professor Boyd Dawkins on the water supply of War- rington • was read:" - Why, asked the Coun- cillor, had not this report been put into the hands of members of the Council so that they could see what was going on? From what he had heard, it was a very big scheme, and the sooner the Council knew what it was the sooner they would be able to grasp it. They. did not want it sprung on them. Councillor Craik said he observed an the same agenda that it had been resolved that a motor car be purchased for the use of the department. He did not think this was a time for purchasing a motor car. The Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock): It is very urgent indeed and absolutely essential. It is in connection with the other matter. Councillor Craik : I shall move that this resolution be referred back.
Councillor Gough seconded. He wanted to know when the Council was going to have a motor car 60 that they would all be able to have a run round. (Laughter.) _

The Mayor: This is going to cut down ex- penditure. Councillor Chrimes suggested that the Borough crest might be painted on the car, as well as a declaration, "This is the pro- perty of the Warrington Corporation." That would prevent the joy-rides of which Coun- cillor Gough was afraid. Councillor Lindley said that suggestion could easily be adopted. It was a motor car and lorry combined, being easily convertible. It was mainly to be used for running about the outlying district with pipes and would be of great economy. A motor car was a necessity at this time of day. Councillor Dickenson thought a Warrington instead of a Rochdale firm should have the order; and the Mayor replied that as it was a Ford car the Warrington agent would get the commission. That it was purchased out of town made no ,difference in that respect. Alderman - Tinnion remarked that the only objection he had to the car was that it was a': Ford and an American. Ile thought they xuight have bought a good second-hand Eng-,1 lish car.

Alderman John Evans the chairman of tilt committee) replied that tile Ford car was most suittOle, With regard to .the Dawkins' report refeiwd to by Councillor Gough, he said the reason it was not mentioned to the Council was because it was now in the hands of Mr. Gray, the engineer, who was preparing an et- haustive report on the matter. At the very earliest opportunity it would be placed in the hands of ,the Council. _ _
The motor car amendment was lost and the vehicle will be purchased.

div.head: HONOURING THE DEAD.
div.p: HONOURING THE DEAD.
Memorial Service To Fallen Bold Street Heroes.

The memory of . those who have fallen was honoured at .Sunday night's service at Bold- street Wesleyan Church, the Rev. Percy meson delivering an inspiring sermon. One .of the obscure promises of sacred writ was, he said, " I will give unto thee treasures of darkness:" To-day there-'was a new mean- ing for those words; for, in this time of gloom and horror, :.there was being revealed a treasure of counyless price. We never knew the worth' and heroism of the motherhood Of this country as we do to-day. The. crown and glory of .our national life was the unflinching bravery of our womankind. In recent days he had gone to sym- pathise with. those who had lost loved ones, but had felt when. lie had met them that to utter any word of sympathy would be to insult them. He felt he was. treading on hallowed ground. The very light of heaven could be seen in, those tear-filled eyes. We would have to tread the lonely years without tie smile of the loved one's face to help,. Those By*, could not be replaced. Sometimes we wonder 4 why they had never had their chance in life. We felt we needed them so much. But had it ever struck one how little people to-day questioned the fact that the dead were not dead after all? There had .come to us another " treaSpre of darkness," a renewed conviction that there was a life after death. Those whom. we • had' loved arc in the Divine Presence. They served him day and night in His. temple. There were some mothers present, and one especially, in . whose heart there was a profound gratitude, because -the , lad who had gone definitely followed Jesus Christ. Christ did 31ot make their „lives uarrow or wool. Ile
did not rob them of any good thing. Nay, lie added untold riches to their lives. To-dayithere was up bitterness in our memory of them, no doubt, only a deep thankfulness.
- Albert Gartland. Of Albert Gartland, for instance, we could say:

"'He had not wearied of life's dusty ways, He looked not to the end, nor sought foirest, As men. do seek when sorrow-laden days Have slain the lust of life within the breast; Without the ministry of one home hand He faced the last and worst, and now for him There is the mourning of the motherland, Proud of the son for whom her eyes are dim."

About such as these there was no doubt. And concerning those whom we spoke of as not religious: "Leave we their souls to God, we bear in mind The duty simply done, the danger braved; Trust in the larger hope and wait to find— 'For him who loseth life shall life be saved.'"

It was not for us to judge. How He dealt with such of His children we did not know, but we might be quite sure that Be greeted them with infinite love. They, too. were in the presence of God, and would find in that Presence oppor- tunities for the Greater Service. Our loved ones still knew all about us, still loved us, and were permitted to help. us in our time of stress and temptation. More than once he had heard it said v" My lad is nearer to me now than ever lie was when I thought of him in the trenches." They were' engaged in the Greater Servce; they served Him day and night in His temple. Their ability to serve would, he fancied, be in propor- tion to the strength of their lives here. That was U.w importauco of this life.

div.head: SOME SUGGESTIONS TO THE TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: SOME SUGGESTIONS TO THE TOWN COUNCIL.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—We have proof on record of a man's selfless interest in his native lown, and "The Examiner" is to be congratulated on the very interesting article under the heading "Orford Hall for Warrington" by Mr. Arthur Moun- field, and the excellent photograph produced. The people of Warrington need feel proud of such men as Alderman Bennett, although we know of others who have served their native town from the inside and outside of its Council Chamber. We honour all of them, bear he Or she the name of Itylands, Smethurst, Crosfield, Greenall, Joseph or Peacock. Some day our noble King will add lustre to his reign by.estab- lishing distinguished 'Orders of Merit" to the good men and women who give of the best years of their lives to their native town with only one object in view, "to make their own people more contentedly happy." There might go with these "Civic Honours" a freedom to use our electric clirs for the remainder of their lives. I hope this suggestion will not end its career in "The Examiner."

We who well know the history of these men of service must often wonder of Warrington: "Would that fine structure across the Mersey; wider streets and open spaces, the Victoria Park —would these things have been in evidence in 1916 if Alderman Bennett had not entered the Council Chamber nearly 25 years ago?" He was chaffed at as "only a dreamer," but has not he been the pioneer of invention which has helped to bring about the bluer sky? Warrington has too long delayed its tribute to its first Mayor, and the name of " Belmont" has done more for the native town thdt. anyone of past or present days!

Let our Town Conn re-christen Orford Hall the " Beament Park War Memorial Home" and let it become— a branch of the great "Kitchener Army" Memorial—a home of peace and comfort for the brave fellows Of the South Lancashire Regiment who have suffered beyond repair for their King and country. If net this, then let it be utilised as a training home for the boys of the fathers who belonged to the South • Lancashire Regiment and who have fallen in the great war of 1914-17. These boys in the " Beament Park War Memorial Home" might be- trained for a commercial career in the great countries of our Allies. The lm- guages of Russi4,..irranee 'and Italy might ,be taught, .vo that they could become invaluable to Great Britain and her Colonies, and thereby increase, the trade with our great Allies., If this-plan is considered feasible, then I suggest a deputation consisting of the Member of the Borough, the Mayor, Sir Gilbert Greenall or Mr. Charles E. Parker, Mr. W. Peter Rylands and Alderman Bennett should arrange an inter- view with the Committee of the "Lord Kitchener Memorial Fund" to obtain a grant towards the upkeep of the " Beam Ont Park War Memorial Home."—Yours, &c., A. J. BROWNER. December 6th, 191 c.

When the Town Council considered on Tuel- day whether they should accept Orford Hall on behalf of the borough there were bah generous appreciation of the donors and the gift and also an attempt to persuade the Council to decline the offer. In this latter Councillors Crailc., and Gough were the prime and only movers. Their attitude led to a lively discussion.

pointed out that the gift originally included twelve acres of land, the hall, and the farm, but Alderman Bennett begged a further six acres, which perhaos might be called a swamp. It was not, however, true to say that the 12 acres were even damp land. So far as his re- collection went—and he could go back, he fancied, forty years—this was the first time in the history of the borough—with the exception of . Bank Park—that contributions had been made by local gentlemen in order to secure such a gift. While giving every credit to Councillors Craik and Gough • for sincerity, their attitude appeared very ungracious. It was unfortunate when a gift of that character —which Was worth every-penny of the 5.,3,600— was made to the town, that they should im- mediately begin, not only to look.the gift horse in the mouth, but. to throw cold water on the swamp. (Laughter.) Alderman Bennett had, had the thankless task of tramping up and down other men's stairs, meeting with disap- pointments, rebuffs and refusals, yet when he had obtained the gift of Orford Hall it was described as another of his white. elephants. It was said that he had foisted white elephants on them before; at any rate, he had never -Previously begged a white elephant for them. (Laughter.) He .had held that the ideal ele- ment in Alderman Bennett out-balanced the practical, but on this occasion he took off his hat to him because he believed that he had shown industrious, persistent and practical effort in the public service. (Hear, hear.)

The. Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) moved the reCommendation of the General Purposes Committee: (1) That the offer be gratefully accepted and that the hearty thanks of the Coun- cil be tendered to, the donors for: their' generous and beneficent gift, and (2)that the best thanks. of the Council be offered to 'Alderman Bennett for his untiring energy and efforts in acquiring Orford Hall and grounds for the town, and that a .copy of this resolution, suitably engrossed, be presented to the Alderman. The Mayor said this .was the most important resolution which had ever come before'the com- mittee during his Mayoralty. They had already three historic buildings in Warrington which had been acquired for public purposes, Bank Hall (now" the Town Hall); the 'Old Acadeniy, and the Old Warps, but on each occasion they had to find a large amount of money'. Orford Hall was a fite gift, and it ,went to the credit largely of Alderman ,Bennett, who had been working at it so energetically for the last twelve months with the objet of securing the hall and grounds for the town. (Applause.) -He thought he had given it up as a bad job-si.x months ago, and the letter he (the Mayor) received a fort- night ago giving the result of his labours' was, therefore, particularly gratifying. Very. few restrictions, ,if they could be called restrictions, were attached to the gift. Colonel Ireland Blackburne had stated in effect that if they kept ,the. fabric in order they could de any convert- ing necessary to meet their 'requirements after the War. After going into the matter with. the Borough Surveyor, he believed that the fears of those who anticipated that a heavy outlay would be required; would prove to be unfounded. At all events, the sanction of the Council would have to be given before any alterations could be carried out. 'The town ought to be very grate- ful to the donors for the handsome gift of this historic hall and to Alderman- rtennett for the untiring energy he had thrown into the project. (Applause.) -Councillor Lindley .seconded the, motion.

div.head: COUNCILLOR GOUGH OBJECTS.
div.p: COUNCILLOR GOUGH OBJECTS.

Councillor Gough would not let the opportu- nity go without criticising this project, which had been praised up sky-high. It had been pointed out, that no. conditions were attached to the gift. It yeauired'no conditions at the price which the donors had paid. They all felt de- lighted at the public spirit which had been shOwn by gentlemen in Warrington in raising the money to purchase the land for a public park and recreation ground and the hall for the bene- fit it was suggested of our lads who were fight- ing to preserve the honour and glory of the British race. He agreed that nothing was too good for our soldiers and their children. (Hear, hear.) Although Orford Hall had been consid- ered of local historical interest, and although it was suitable for, the Mune in turn of the Norris family, John Blackburne, a distinguished botan- ist, and William Beamont, the first Mayor of Warrington, he submitted that it was not worth the price paid for it, £3,600. Why was not the Property put up for public sale by auction? It had been in the market long enough. A few years ago it was offered to the.:Corporation, but the Council refused to purchase because the land was not considered suitable for a park and recreation ground. ("Na.") ,If it was not con- sidered: suitable at that time, what had hap- pened since' to make it suitable? For months every year the land was under water; if was, full of pools, ditches, and brooks, and to drain it would mean a very considerable drain on the rates of the borough. (Laughter.) If that were the case, this free gift might 'eventually turn out a very costly luxury. He did not believe the Corporation were viewing the subject from a business standpoint. It would be more cor- rect to say they regarded it as a matter of sen- timent, because of the ancestral associations Of the hall, and in order to perpetuate. the name of some distinguished botanist, who might be a very interesting person in his day, but in whom very few were interested now—unless it were Alderman. Bennett. (Laughter.) The hall would cost at least £l,OOO for repairs to make it anything like suitable for a museum or a social club. If a hall were required for educa- tional or social purposes why not utilise the one in Victoria Park, which was now let at .220 per annum, but which et one time was praised sky- high. Would the Council give an undertaking that they would not spend on the hall and land more than £5,000 in the next 'ten years--that would be £5OO a year? Ile moved that the offer be not accepted. The Mayor: You move that it be referred back to the committee? ; Councillor Gough: Yes.

div.head: SCHEME DUBBED A "WHITE
div.p: SCHEME DUBBED A "WHITE
ELEPHANT."

Councillor Craik seconded the amendment, because he 'honestly believed the- property dear as a gift. The land was nothing but a swamp, and was not fit for a park. He believed the cost of putting Orford Hall in anything like a fit condition for any purpose whatever would cost a very considerable amount of money. He looked .upon it as one of Alderman Bennett's,'"white elephants." (" Oh l") He had foisted one Or two on the town, and he hoped the - Council would not accept this one.

div.head: COUNCILLOR HENSHALL HITS HARD.
div.p: COUNCILLOR HENSHALL HITS HARD.

Councillor Hensball replied to the objectors in a cimvincing • speech, in the course of which he was frequently interrupted by Councillor Goufh. The latter gentleman was called to order several tithes by the Mayor. Councillor Hen Shall thought that after the discussion at the General Purposes Committee and the visit which members of the Council paid to Orford. Hall the previous day, Coun- cillor Gough, Who certainly had the courage of his convictions—(l4ughter)—Would have remem- bered. what Oliver Cromwell wrote in a bit of a pet to one of the generals who was worrying him, "I would to God that ye would think it pes- sible that ye might be -mistaken." (Laughter.) That never seemed to have dawned on Council- lor Gough. It • was •an absolute untruth to call the land .a swamp.
C'onncillor Gough: Why couldn't they sell it, thert?
The Mayor They are giving it us, which is far better.
Henshall said that at the meeting of the General. Purposes Committee it was

div.head: Cross-Talk
div.p: Cross-Talk

Continuing, Councillor Henshall said that there was no better land in the town as re- garded twelve acres of it for the purposes of .a park. Councillor Gough: Nonsense. Councillor Henshall : I fancy I know as much about land as Councillor Gough. Councillor_ Gongh : I would not 'give 11,000 for it.
Councillor Henshall : I daresay you would not give anything for it. Councillor Gough: No, I would not.

Councillor Hen-shall : That is. nonsense. You don't know what you are talking about. For the sake of argument, the Councillor went on, strip the site of the ball and farm and look upon it as bare land, And it could be laid out in a most attractive, economical manner. Councillor Gough: Was it ever cultivated? The Mayor: Do behave yourself. Councillor Henshall : Councillor Gough has never been cultivated. I don't know about the land. (Loud laughter.) The speaker went on to show that the land was in close proximity to several 'working-class wards, and, as a park, its situation was. beautiful. As to its value, he would ask what the Council had given far other land in the town. They wanted a. site for a school in the immediate neighbourhood of Orford Hall, and they gave 'over .2900 an acre for it. (Councillor Gough: "Shame.") They wanted three acres of land at the other end of the town for a school, and they gave over .21,000 an acre.
Councillor Gough: That was the Education Committee.

Councillor -Henshall : It was a committee of the Council. They then 'wanted land, in. the immediate neighbourhood of the school for recreation purposes, and 'it cost over ..2po an acre, though it was ,the cheapest land the Corporation ever bought for such • an area; while for . the land which the "Council acquired for a school and recreation ground in Lovely-lane—roughly seven acres—they paid nearly £6,000 —S,B(W. he -cOst, of the land Which was now so genereusly presented to the town worked out at only .2200 per acrei Another reason why he Submitted that-the price was low was that a- committee of the Town Council several years ago carefully Fonsidered the pur- chase of the land. They were asked something like £6,000 for it, and they refused to pay it— not because the land was unsuital)l, but they thought the price too high and actually offered £4,000. Surely' if it were worth that sum 8 years ago it was a travesty of language and the very marrow of ingratitude to talk of it as a white elephant to-day.. He believed the gift, if they properly appreciated it, would only be the be- ginning of other gifts in order that their chil- dren might breathe purer air and have ampler space. (Applause.)

div.head: POSSIBLE USES.
div.p: POSSIBLE USES.

Alderman James Evans was alsct enthusiastic over the gift, for which he said they should be deeply grateful. He added that Orford Hall was formerly looked upon as the most ancient and aristocratic of the 'residences to be found anywhere about the town. (Hear, hear.) The spot was an ideal one. There was no doubt that when the war was over there would be a need for a home for those who would be without one, and who, had been sorely wounded in 'their country's service. An obligation would rest on the Council and on the citizens to make some provision for the lads who would be 'crippled, disabled, and deserve all the care and comfort 'Which could be provided for them. Further, there were children for whom nothing ,had been done at present, and the day was not far dis- tant when the Government would perhaps force the hands of the Council in this respect a little more than they were doing at present. It would be part of the duty of the Town Council, as the education authority, to put as much sunshine ' and pleasure as possible into the lives of the unfortunate little ones. (Hear, hear.) A maternity home would have to be provided which would be worthy of the town, and ho was of opinion that if the Council had no other' object in view than this, it was their duty to secure Orford Hall. (Hear, hear.) Again and again in that chamber the needs of the town had been clearly put forward, and complaints had been made that no generous soul had put their hands into their pockets to supply those needs, and help the town out of their difficulties. Now several gentlenien, whose names appeared in, the minutes, had recognised that Orford Hall would be of value to the town, or they would not have subscribed so handsomely to purchase it. (Hear, hear.) Here generosity had been shown in as nice 'a form as had ever been displayed, and yet an amendment had been submitted—he wished to speak plainly—which would be re- 'corded, and which would indicate, that there was a measure of ungrateful feeling on the part of some of the members. He hoped the amend- nient would not be pressed,' as he would not like it to be put on the records of the town. (Hear, hear;) The least the Council could do was t., accept the offer, and Alderman Bennett de- served the thanks not only of the Council, but Of the town, for his untiring efforts. (A - plause.) COUNCILLOR WILKINSON'S. ASSURANCE
Councillor Wilkinson could not remember

div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT HITS OUT AT OPPONENTS.
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT HITS OUT AT OPPONENTS.

Alderman Bennett was indignant about the criticism offered, but hoped the donors of the hall and land would be as undisturbed' as he, personally, had been. , They certainly would be if they knew_ Councillor Gough as well as the Council knew him. He, believed the time would come when Councillor Gough would be. glad if he could blot out the words he had uttered that evening. (Hear, hear.) He did not know .what the voters in his ward would think of him. As for Councillor Craik, in whose judgment he generally ..placed confidence,;Alderman ..Bennett said he could not account for the obliquity of his judgment on this occasion. Perhaps it was the lighting restrictions ,which had affected him.

(Laughter.) It was not the real Councillor Craik to take up sttch an attitude. (Hear, hear.) - It was quite unnecessary to say one word in reference to the arguments which had been put forward that evening against the purchase; as they had been completely pulverised by his friends who had already spoken. There was, therefore, only ene thing he wished to say, and that was to call attention to the fact that Colonel Blackburne liVed amid this so-called swamp, and died there at the age of 93;- that Mr. William Beamont,. the first Mayor of Warring- ton, lived there for 'many years, and died in his 92nd year; while Mrs. Beamont did not pass away until she was 88. These were facts which spoke • for \themselves. (Hear, hear, and applause.) How anyone could dare to elaini to represent the citizens of. Warrington' who showed such abysmal ignorance as Councillor Gough had displayed in ' every detail of this matter of Orford Hall passed his (Alderman Bennett's) comprehension.. As for Councillor Gough's contention that nothing had been culti- vated at Orford Hall, he (Alderman Bennett) pointed .out that there was in the Museum a , catalogue of thousands of plants grown in the garden of "John Blackburne, Esq.; Orford Hall," in the year, 1789.. "I have often been good-naturedly taunted as a dreamer," he added, "but my best reward for public life- has been in finding; every now and then, some cherished dream achieved. Orford Hall is one of the oldest and the dearest dreams. of all. . The place has appealed to me from my boyhood. My father has often de- scribed to me the noble aVenue of trees which led to it, and which I can just remember in the days of their decrepitude; but the obelisk which stood at the top of the avenue is still a vivid reeollection in my • mind, and „it seemed to me to be a sort of sacrilege to remove it. For the grand old botanist to twhom it was erected—in spite of Councillor Gough's ignor- ant jeers—deserves commemorating, and monu- ments in Warrington are all too few. Happily, here is a better monument, and not to him alone, but to all the 'family, and especially to his generous descendant, Colonel Robert Ire- land Blackburne, as well as to the Peamonts and the other well-known local families so hon- ourably connected with the town.

div.head: Tribute To Donors.
div.p: Tribute To Donors.

"But, altogether apart from its historical associations, which, as I have said, go back for over six centuries, we wanted a , park and re- creation ground for that part of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) I once described it as a wilder- ness of bricks and mortar,' and the words were something more than a mere figure of speech. Its crowded population are sorely in need of. a place of rest .and recreation; where the old olks may sit in the sunshine, 'remembering ancient days,' and the younger generation find facilities for the healthy and innocent enjoy- ment they require, which will, I hope, include a lake for bathing, boating and skating. The hall itself is a beautiful old building, as those of you who visited it yesterday would realise,- ' and might readily be applied to various useful purposes. '`l ventured to 'suggest a few in my letter, and I could easily 'suggest as many more; but I am confident that the Corporation will be able, in due course, to. turn it to some appropriate use. You have thanked- me all too generously for the part which it has been my humble privilege to play in the transaction, but your deepest thanks areAue to the. men whose generosity, in a time. ,of exceptional t stress and strain, has made the offer possible. (Hear; hear.) 1 find it difficult adequately to express. my sense qf obligation to Colonel Blackburne; to Sir Gilbert Greenall, to Mr: Charles E. Parker, to the Walker family, and to Messrs. William Mortimer and Co., for their kindness, and I cannot refrain from taking this public opportunity of tendering my warmest thanks to Mr. H. Beresford ,Melville, to Mr. Henry Greenall, and to Mr. J. J. Whitley for their valuable 'help and counsel in the matter. In spite of your objection to tablets, Mr. Mayor —(laughter)—l trust that the names, of the donors will be suitably recorded somewhere on the 'building, in order that posterity may re- member its benefactors; and I devoutly hope that this 'memorial of the valour of the lads of Warrington.- in the great war' may Tiring health and happiness and inspiration to all the generations yet to come." (Applause.) Alderman Tinnion also spoke ,enthusiastically of the, gift. _ _

When- the Mayor Was about to put the amendment to the vote; Alderman James Evans and Councillor rienshall appealed to Council- lors Craik and Gough to withdraw their oppo- sition, but they shook their heads negatively. ,On the vote being taken they had: no supporters and :the hall was. accepted amidst applause by, the other members of the Council.

In doing justice to him and •his services, the country may remember that the same unscrupulous methods which have succeeded in mak- ing him, our most experienced statesman, a" spectator," were applied, though unsuccessfully, to undermine the authority of LORD KITCHENER, when in the midst of the most gigantic task ever undertaken by a British soldier. But whatever we may think of the methods by which the changes of this week have been brought about, we are confronted by dn accomplished fact. div.p: GOSSIP.
Those who have any railway travelling to do had better get it done. It is stated that fares will be up 50 per cent. in the New Year—not
a " happy " prospect by .any means,
The Watch Committee have commended P.C. Cameron (78) for his action in stopping a run- away'horse. Peace hath it. heroes, no lesd re- nowned than war.
I see an attempt is being made to whiten gable ends and other places that are dangerous obstructions in the dark.

Unless we are supplied with some means of evading these obstructions, which are excep- tionally numerous in Warrington, we shall soon have as many casUaltiest.at home as abroad: Split heads, lost teeth and damaged limbs are getting far too many.
I wonder if the police have heard anything of the mean thefts that are becoming unconf- fortably frequent at the Cemetery.

A few hours after the interment of the late Mr. John Booth last week it; was found that all the wreaths on the grave had been stripped, of the ribbons by which they had bocrt bound by loving hands. Nexii to -flowers had been stolen from a grave that had been adorned by a be- reaved husband and son. •
I might be dubbed German if I suggested the punishment I would deallut ta these wretched ghouls if I had them iWrmy power.. Robbing the dead is surely the end Of. everything. '
'The best thanks of the Parks Committee have ,been given to Mr.. J. Chailtou Parr for a gift of three ducks for the pond. Two swans from the river will join them to-day. -
Councillor Craik has resigned from member- ship of the Ga 4 Committee, and the Mayor has been appointed in his stead.

A resolution of St. Helens Town Council call- ing upon the Government to increase the separation allowances of wives and dependents of soldiers has been adopted by the Warring- ton Town Council.
Councillor Gough was the butt of as severe a piece of repartee as was ever heard in the Conn- cil Chamber.
Not content with having said all he could against Orford Hall and the land on which it stands, he did his best to prevent Councillor Henshall from saying what could he said on.the other side.

Interruption followed interruption by Coun- cillor Gough, in spite of the Mayor's oft re- peated request that he should listen as others listened to him. At length the following little passage, which delighted an outraged council, was heard :
Councillor Gough (to Councillor Henshall, who was speaking as to the value of the hare land without the hall ancl.farm): Has it ever been cultivated? -
The Mayor: CouneillOr Gough, behave your- self.
Councillor Henshall: Councillor Gough has not been cultivated.
Councillor Gough was unabashed and inter- rupted to the end.

But when Alderman Bennett came on to the scene he was too quick for Councillor Gough, and declared-that it passed his comprehension to understand how any man dare display in public such abysmal ignorance as Councillor Gough had displayed.

div.head: PROMOTED POSTMASTER.
div.p: PROMOTED POSTMASTER.
Mr. H. C. Jones Going To Abergavenny.

In having been appointed as postmaster at Abergavenny, the gateway of Wales, Mr. Her- bert Conway Jones, chief. clerk at. ,the Warring- ton Post Office, has received well-earned promo- tion. He has been associated with the Civil Service in his native town for 36 years, and dur- ing his lifetime has Witnessed and taken part in many developments in .the Post Office system. When he entered the service in 1880 there were only twenty delivering postmen, whereas now there are no fewer than 90. The activities of the Post Office have also widened from the mere simplicity of receiving and delivering letters, th% sale of money. and postal orders, and the Savings Bank Department. In addition there have been the parcels post, the administration of the .01d Age Pensions Act, Income Tax, the Insurance Act, and the Payment of. War Allow- ances; the transfer of the telephone system to the Post Office, and the removal of the War- rington Post Office itself from Sankey-street to Springfield-street.
Mr. Jones will move from one new office into another, that at Abergaveany having been opened as recently as May, 1915, and it is said to be one of the best Post Offices of the South

div.head: MR. IT. C. JONES.
div.p: MR. IT. C. JONES.

Wales area. Of all phases of POst.Office work Mr. Jones has had experience. He started as a sorter; went through the usual routine of pro- motion by stages until on the sth • December, 1901, he succeeded Mr. J. K. Broadhurst, on that gentleman's appointment as Postmaster at Ashton-under-Lyne.

Mr. Jones was educated at the People's Col- lege under the late Mr. Twiss, who has tutored many men who have taken prominent positions in life. Devoted almost exclusively to his work-, Mr. Jones has had little time for menabership of various local societies, but be has been con- nected with the Freemasons of the "Gilbert Greenall " Lodge, 1250, and also with Bold-street Methodist Church. He, has two sons, one Mr. Stanley Jones, who is an assistant master at Silver-street Schools, and the 'other Mr. Harold Ivan Jones, of the Lancashire and :Yorkshire Bank.
Mr. Jones commences his new duties on January Ist.

div.head: CALL FOR UNITY.
div.p: A CALL FOR UNITY.
MOB LAW.
Wk. Charles Parker And Mr. Roberts's German Reasoning.
"WHAT OF THE FUTURE?
To the Editor of "The Examiner."
Sir,—l desire to make my protest against the mew form of law which is being introduced into Warrington for the suppression by force a meetings.

In the first place, I would make my own position clear. I am at one with Mr. Henry Roberts when -he says: tinder present condi- tions any peace with Germany is impossible." And, further, that at the present time it may he " ridiculous " to talk about peace at all. At the moment we have all something better to do, and if every individual made it his first and paramount duty to do his best in further- ing the vigorous prosecution of the war, I fancy he will have neither time nor energy to dis- cuss terms of, peace. But none of us have the right to attempt by force to dictate to others what they should think and do. We have no right to say that they ,shall not meet together to bear an address on " How to secure a People's Peace."

div.head: QUESTION OF RESPONSIBILITY.
div.p: QUESTION OF RESPONSIBILITY.

It is very easy for Mr. Henry Roberts to say, as he did to the Mayor, " I must again repeat our determination to take no responsibility for what may happen if the meeting is proceeded with." In the first place, nothing would have happened if Mr. Roberts and his friends had ignored the meeting, and, in the second, Mr. Roberts cannot by such a statement evade the responsibility of his own. acts. If an individual wilfully prepares all the conditions which make for disorder, strife, and perhaps bloodshed; he has. no right to say he accepts no responsi- bility; the responsibility is his, and his alone. It would be as opportune for tile German Chancellor to have said—as he did , in effect say----" We will 'march through Belgium; if the Belgians object and resist it is our determina- tion to 'take no responsibility for what may happen," If those who organised this demon- stration had the. law behind them they would have had some little justification, but the keeping of the peace happily does not rest with self-appointed guardians, lint with the Chief of the Police, and ultimately with the Home Secretary.

Mr. Samuel, the Home Secretary, dealing with the Merthyr Tydvil meetings, took the wise and right line. He said: "I am unwilling to use the powers vested in me to suppress its meetings," He refused to forbid the meetings at Merthyr, and. presumably, at Warrington, on grounds of sound policy. Mr. Roberts and his associates, in opposition to the decision of th.e Home Secretary, took upon themselves tO suppress the meeting, with the result that they have given an advertisement to, the Peace Propaganda, and, as the Home Secretary says, "done something to mislead the -world :into thinking that the Pacifist Movement in this eountry is so formidable that it is necessary to suppress it." Mr. Samuel further adds: TO secure .by threats of disorder the , suppression by force of law of meetings, however wrong- headed those meetings may be, would not be helpful," and- he expresses the- hope that Mr. Stanton (the organiser of the suggested oppo- sition in Wales) may be willing and able to induce his supPOrters to 'ignore the holding of the conference in the town and to deprive it of the advertisement which disturbances wOuld give. Mr.. Stanton .wisely accepted the advice: and it is a pity Mr. Roberts did not show like wisdom.

div.head: VALUE OF SPIRITUAL AND MORAL FORCES.
div.p: VALUE OF SPIRITUAL AND MORAL FORCES.

It should be remembered that 'what have given driving power to this country in the war are the spiritual and moral forces behind all that is material. The outrages and violation of the laws of God and man by the Germans at the beginning, and, indeed, all through the conflict, has given strength to our arms. ho not let us now lower our ideals and drag Our honour in. the mire by copying the Germans in their use of force, unsupported by justice or right. In every church and chapel in our borough we have at all services prayers for peace. In the name of the congregation the clergyman or minister asks God that He would hasten the time When peace shall reign. They pray: "Give peace in our time, 0 Lord, we ask it in the name of Him who is the Prince of Peace,, Jesus Christ our Lord." No protest is ever made to such prayers. They are approved as the expression of a general desire and endorsed with silent and often, articulate "Amens" ! What .a strange paradox. We are at liberty to talk to God about .peace, to pray for a People's Peace' in which the universal fatherhood of God and the consequent universal brotherhood of Man is recognised; but when anyone comes to talk to a public, or, rather, semi-private meeting, not to God,. but to men, about a. "People's Peace," then such a gathering is suppressed by Mob Law, and the opposers are led and inspired by Justices of the Peace.

div.head: MISTAKEN POLICY.
div.p: A MISTAKEN POLICY.

Tbe action taken, if not illegal in itself, was likely to result in illegal acts. It was contrary to the desire of, the highest legal authority;' it was .mistaken in policy and calculated to pro- duce the opposite results to those the promoters had in View. and it has set an evil example, which Warrington in the future may have bitter cause to regret. It may well be that in the future Mr. Roberts may be in the minority and his views forcibly suppressed, and should he protest, his protests will be laughed to scorn and he will be reminded that he himself established the precedent—Yours, &c.,
CHARLES E. PARKER.
December Cth, 1916

div.head: MR. MAGINN'S IDEALS.
div.p: MR. MAGINN'S IDEALS.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."
Sir,—Events both ominous and inspiring have crowded. on us so fast this week that it behoves every man Who loves liberty to put his best into the common .Stock.-
My letter (to which you so kindly gave pro- minence last week) commenting on the new magisterial appointments, has been regarded by some as striking a dissentient note.

It was not my intention that it should. I .wrote it as a. protest against partiality— partiality which is a fruitful cause of dissen- sion—and as such I hope the vast majority of your readers regarded it.

THE INTERESTS OF PUBLIC SAFETY. If ever there was a time when dissension should be hushed in the interests of public safety it is now. If ever there was a time when every .eitizen of. the British Empire should put ,his *hole strength at the service of the State, now is the time. I hope I am not a coward, and I do not wish to pOSe as an alarmist; but I think the cause of civilisation is in danger, and the British Empire is in danger. We are faced at present by two Malignant enemies—the German hosts, and our own tendency to quarrel amongst ourselves. Vdeplore, the invasion of the elementary. hut sacred right of free speech successfully engineered . in Warrington last Friday. . We !rare introducing the Gentian doctrine of "lese Majeste" in a very dangerous form. hope other towns will not follow the evil precedent set up by those who coerced the Friends to cancel their little indoor meeting. To invoke the unreasoning anger Of the crowd is always easy in times of excitement; .but to allay it or °Control it is very difficult, and sometimes im- possible. Besides, there are much nobler ways of. displaying patriotism than the silencing of free discussion. • '

But this local example of illegal interference with the liberty of the subject is only a. small symptom of a rampant evil presently showing itself in high places .and low in -this country. I mean the deplorable disposition to hunt for scapegoats. Our misfortunes in the war;' our blunders, delays and incompetence are not so bad but that they can be remedied if we clear. our minds, preserve our -unity, and organise and discipline our strength. But if we resort to the savage device of organising -Witch-liunts —"smelling out. witches," as Rider. Haggard has it—as a way • of warding off defeat, we shall never triumph over our German foe.

div.head: IMMINENT DANGER.
div.p: IMMINENT DANGER.

The position in which the country finds itself to-day is too serious-.--th, • danger is too imminent for it to be safe for us to indulge in spites and. hatreds. A new National 'Govern- ment has been formed to cope :with the mighty task imposed on us. The Allies are the Guardians. of Liberty • and • Justice, and they must triumph or .perish. Do we all 'realise this, or are we going to dissipate our energies by more -internal • quar- rels and fratricidal strife?
To attain any good end to this war, domestic disputes, greed selfishness • and intolerance must immediately cease

I do not care flow the National Government is composed; or who leads it. If it will. call all sections to its support impartially, and show that it means business; then it deserves the prompt and willing service of. every lover of Freedom and Justice.

div.head: NATIONAL SOLIDARITY.
div.p: NATIONAL SOLIDARITY.

I should like to see Warrington initiate a movement to . secure- national solidarity. I would suggest to his 'Worship the 'Mayor to call' a nieetinft of responsible citizens - of 'every class to further unity of action,, and to •dis courage all • tendencies to' disruption and in.• ternal strife. Apportioning' the blame for what is past will avail nothing. Resolute and united support of the National Ministry will yet conquer.—Yours, &c.; •
F. It_k.C4INN.

div.head: DRAMATIC INCIDENT,
div.p: DRAMATIC INCIDENT,
Old Wound Opened At Food Conference.
TRADE UNIONIST RECRIM- INATIONS.

There was a dramatic incident towards the close of the Food Prices Conference in the Co- operative Hall on Thursday night, when there. was a breeze between Mr. Edwin Plinston, chairman (also chairman- Of the Trades and Labour Council), and Mr. Joseph Elwell, of the Iron and Steel Workers Association, who, it will be recollected, seceded from the Trades Council on the ground that the latter .body is Socialistic., A resolution had been moved by the Trades Council asking for increased wages, and Mr. Elwell asked how these were to be got. - The Chairman (heatedly):. I hope we are a sufficiently strong body, of Trade Unionists in Warrington to take it Up. I hope all Unions are hot made of _political parties.

Up jumped-31r. Elwell, • fired with indigna- tion, and. declared: "I object to that. I say that as an association the iron and steel workers are freer than any other association in Warling- ton from party politics-. As an association we Lave never been connected with party politics. Every member has, been at liberty to choose for himself, and I object to Any insinuation like that." '

The Chairman, who by obvious effort had cooled himself, retorted: "I Ath not thinking of him as an iiidividu#l, or of the association he is connected with, and I don't. know Why he should become so fiery."' .

• Mr. Elwell gathered. up his papers, and walked out. As he passed the reporters' table he said .he was disgusted. The conference consisted of delegates from all the Unions in the town, as Well as several Societies, and it was well attended. There were nearly a dozen ladies as delegates. The out- come of it was that the conference passed a reso- lution calling unon the Mayor to call a fown's meeting at which the following resolution (sug- gested by the Trades Council and passed as a substantive motion) will be presented: " That this conference, viewing with alarm the con- tinued increase of food prices? and the conse- quent poverty of the people !resulting there- froth, do hereby express, our denunciation of the inactivity of the Government to deal with this vital question, and requests organised labour to demand increased wages equivalent to the increased Cost of 'food as the only solution to this most pressing :question which is .draw- ing upon the life's blood of the Mass of the community."
The next resolution came from the Warring- ton Co-operative Sbeiety, who "welcomed- the attempt • of the Co-operative Movement' to obtain access to the source 'of supply of, raw materials." .

A resolution, from the Iron and Steel Workers, Association urged "that the timohas now come when the Government should take strong meagures to restrict:advances and regulate the price of food. Also wlere there is evidence of, exploitation of the people's food, those respon- sible' for such exploitation to he dealt with in the Strongest possible manner." On a. vote being taken the Trades Council's resolution •received 45 votes; ' Co-oßerative Society's, 11; and the Iron and Steel Worwers, 9. The Trades Council's, motion' was then car- ried as a substantive one. •

div.head: HOSPITAL SUNDAY.
div.p: HOSPITAL SUNDAY.
E) Thc Churches Give Fair Share To institutions ?

Are the Warrington and District Churches contributing a fair quota to the local Infirm- ary? The question, was discussed at a meeting of the Hospital Sunday Committee, held on Friday afternoon last week at the Infirmary, Mr. J. H. Smethurst presidin;g. The Chairman said he would not be the man he thought himself if he expressed his satisfac- tion with the collections taken on Hospital. Sun- day throughout the churchev in the town and diStrict. He thought appeals on behalf of the hospital, which did so much for the sick and suffering, should be more forcibly brought home. There was a deficiency of nearly two thousand pounds on the present year, and they could not afford to run on. in that manner without con- sidering. their position. me Rev. G. C. Briggs, Latchford, thought it should not be forgotten that many of the people who attended the chuiches were already subscribers to the hospital. Whether well-to-do people or working class people, they made equal sacrifices according to their income. Mr. A. .T. Jolley was re-elected hon. Eecre- tary to the committee; on the proposition of Mr. Smethurst, seconded by the Rev. G. C. Briggs, the Rev. W. T. Derry, in supporting, saying that M. Jolley should be backed up better. He had been comparing the collections of some of the churches, and found that some cf them sent an ayerage collection. He thought that that was not at all customary, but that the collecion for the hospital should be the largest of the year.

It was decided to hold Hospital Sunday on March 18th, and, on the proposition of the Rev. G. C. Briggs, to send out circulars, to be placed in the churches a week beforehand, showing the income and expenditure and the number of patients treated each year. The Secretary's report showed that five places of worship which contributed to the fund in 1915 failed to do so in 1916. Six others renewed or commenced contributing; on the balance there was a net gain under the heads of .26 9s. 7d. The total receipts were £265 19s. 3d., a decrease, compared with last,year, of £ll 9s. 3d. Of this amount, £153 15s. Bd. was collected within, and £ll2 3s. 7d. outside-the borough.

div.head: LOWER THAN THE
div.p: LOWER THAN THE
AVERAGE.
Warrington's Record In Venereal Diseases.

On the suggestion of. the Medical Officer 01' Health (Dr. U. W. N. Joseph) a special arrange- ment has been arrived at to treat cases oi venerea) diseases at the Infirmary. In his report to the Town Council on Tuesday the Medical Officer referred to the incidence of the diseases in Warrington, and said that it was impossible to give any definite figures: "But," he added, "the Royal Commission c,ame to the conclusion that the number of persons who have been infected with syphilis acquired or congenital cannot fall below 10 per cent. of the whole population in the large cities, and the percentage affected with gonorrhoea must greatly exceed this proportion.' Now if these figures held good for Warrington it would mean more than 7,000 cases of syphilis and a great many more than that of gonorrhoea. Personally, I do not think we have anything like that amount of disease in this town. Members of the Medical Board here who have examined very large num- bers of all classes of men from this area state that only on extremely rare occasions has a case of venereal disease been found. From in- formation kindly supplied me by the local medical men (21), I have obtained the follow- ing approximate figures of the cases, coming under medical supervision annually :,--Primary syphilis, 110; secondary, 105; tertiary, 150; and gonorrhoea, 212. This, of course, does not take into account the number of cases that refrain, from obtaining medical advice, ',arid' seek- the aid of the chemist, the 'herbalist, or the quack. The difficulty of arriving at anything like a cor- rect estimate of the incidence ,of venereal diseases in. Warrington, as elsewhere., is . insur- mountable, and even if we did knOrty, the 'exit numbers we would still have no knowledge as to the numbers who would avail themselves of the facilities we propose to offer. Under these circumstances, all that can be given is a provi- sional estimate of the expense to be incurred for the first twelve months, after which' period the whole scheme will have to be reviewed in the light of the experience gained here and hi ctber towns."

div.head: LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD TO PAY MOST.

Alderman James Evans, in moving the con- firmation of the minutes of the Health Com- mittee, referred to the local scheme. By the recent regulations, he said, it had been made compulsory for every county borough to draw up a scheme, under which if would be possible' for any member of the community who required it to obtain free of charge the best and most expensive forms of treatment or diagnosis. In the past the cost of this had been prohibitive to a certain section of the public. With regard to the institutional part of the treatment, the com- mittee had already approached the Board of Management of the local Infirmary, and they were prepared to undertake the work. div.head: Conscientious Teacher's War Contribution.
div.p: Conscientious Teacher's War Contribution.
In the case of George J. M. Baker, aged 24, assistant teacher, Society of Friends' School, Penketh,- _

Mr. Furness, Military representative, said this case was very curious. The Tribunal had given him exemption from combatant service on con- scientious grounds. The ease went to Liverpool, where that decision was confirmed, and they sent him to the Friends' Ambulance Unit. In- stead of the Friends taking him on, they sent him back to the Friends' School, and they gave him a certificate for which he (Mr. Furness) maintained they had no authority. They also in- sisted upon the man paying a sum out of his wages to the unit. If e (the Military Repre- sentative) did not think they could make use o and put this man where they liked. The Tri- bunal ought to take notice of the matter. Mr. Baker, a young man of studious and rather delicate appearance, answered the ques- tions put by the Military Representative in the clearest and most intnesting manner. He had been exempted from combatant service, and on appeal to Liverpool was given non-combatant service. He went to join the Friends' Ambu- lance Unit. . They gave him it certificate and sent him to the Friends' School at Penketh. Mr. Furness: And made it a condition that you should send them A:6O a year out of your wages? Mr. Baker said he was to send £6O a year to the Polish Relief Fund. They imOosed the con- dition and he chose the fund himself. They had told him that in the case of men who were allowed to remain, teaching men were to make a considerable sacrffice of income. He offered to pay ,220 each'term to the Polish Relief Fund. He paid it at the end of last term, and intended to pay it at the yid of this term. Mr. Furness said he was not opposidg his grounds as a conscientious objector, but wanted this information to show what grounds they had for making the appeal. A Member: I- take it that he has practically bought himself out of the Artny.
The Chairman: He has made some sacrifice,

Mr. Knowles: Not voluntarily. Mr. Baker said he was required to subscribe to some fund not political and that had nothing to do with the Friends' Society, and he chose the Polish Relief Fund. They did not suggest the amount he should give. _ _ _ _
In reply to the Clerk he said he objected to be medically examined.
The Chairman said they were satisfied that his appeal was honest and straightforward. _ _

Mr.. -Baker said he had been trained as a teacher and educated for a teacher, and found that he was doing most useful work. He had communicated with the Friends' Ambulance Unit, and they were quite prepared for him to undertake other work which would be of national importance. s„ The Clerk read the list of occupations which had been arranged between the War Office and the Friends' Ambulance Unit, and said that of teacher was not amongt them. Mr. Baker gaid that teaching was in the original list, hut had been struck out. Ultimately Mr. Baker's case was adjourned for a fortnight in order to see if he could not find employment of more importance to the nation than that upon which he was engaged at present.

By CRITIC.

The Clerk of the Weather is still in .bad' humour. . Despite what the "'Old Journalist" says about my last remark on this subject, first .we have a short spell of frost, .then we have a spell of rain. ,
And no 'doubt you know the result : slippery roads, slutchy boots,' and, in many cases, right bad colds.
By this time last year we had had two or three days' good skating on the lake.
Several local skating enthusiasts were look- ing forward to a good time this week-end,. but, alas, they were doomed to disappoint- ment.
I came across two young .ladies the .other day. who were busily practising the noble art of nursing.
One, who apparently had a sore finger, was playing the part of "patient," while the other, a strapping girl of some nineteen sum- mers, was eagerly putting her through it.
Judging by the row they were making, I should say they would make " some " nurses.
Just recently I have overheard several people remark that they did not know where to go for advice regarding soldiers'' and • sailors' pensions. - '
If people desiring information on this sub- ject will communicate with Mr. P. E. Evans, he will endeavour to give them the informa- tion required.
I hear that there is to be a special service at the Congregational Church on Sunday evening for the benefit of everyone who has lost any relatives during the present campaign.
The Rev. Shields Gill will deliver a special message, to the "troubled and bereaved."
I notice that the Plotmaster-General has issued a sp2cial appeal to post early before Christmas.
And not to post anything before Christmas that can possibly wait until after.
This appeal has been made necessary by the immense number of Post Office servants who have been called to the Colours—and to the scarcity of ttmporau labour.
What's the Matter in Lymm this week? How is it that things are so slack?
There seems to have been "nothing doing" at all.
I noticed a few more wounded arriving at the Brookfield 'Hospital on Thursday morning.
Will the newly-constructed Cabinet have any immediate effect on the war? That is a question freely discussed at present.
To. use. the late Prime Minister's motto, we will "Wait and see."
I noticed an 'enterprising local grocer yester- day advertising the sale of " War flour" by a large notice in his window.
I suppose it's a way of slowly breaking us in.
• "Everything is going up," was the cry of one housewife the other day. "Even errand running." •
A neighbouring boy who used to run her errands at a penny a time has now informed her that he can no longer do them at the old price, and in future she will have to pay three halfpence.
I suppose this new rise is due to the increased price_ of boots.
Are farmers playing the game? I wonder! A ease relating to exemptions has just been brought to my-notice which makes me doubt it.
I was pleased to see Lieut. Wilde, who is home on furlough, looking so hale and hearty.
It will be remembered that he lost a son in the war a few months ago.
He is at present guarding German prisoners at the Isle of Man camp.

div.head: NOVEL .PARADE.
div.p: A NOVEL .PARADE.
Wounded Soldiers Attend Departure Of Hospital Comrade.

A most unusual scene was witnessed in Lymm last Wednesday, when a party of wouinled soldiers from the Brookfield Hospital marched from the hospital, through the village, and down to the station to witness the departure of one of fhr hospital comrades who was going on his t6i aays' furlough prior to rejoin- ing his unit. The departing soldier was Private Gibbs, who, by his cheerful disposition, has made a host of friends throughout the village. The procession, as it marched on its way, sang Patriotic and 'rag-time • melodies, and did not fail to attract a great, deal of attention. Shell- torn and battle-worn, some on crutches, some without limbs, and all bearing the terrible marks of battle, they marched gaily on, heeding nothing, and only conscious of the fact that they were for a few. minutes extremely happy._ „ _
"I wonder what our Cabinet Ministers would think of themselves and the present crisis could they but see this happy throng?" was a remark heard from an enthusiastic spectator, and it made us wonder.

Arriving at the station, the party, at the in- stigation of one of their leaders, immediately took possession of their departing comrade, placed him on one of the platform seats, and made him give a farewell speech. Amid rous- ing cheers, the soldier meekly obeyed his com- rades' request, and although his speech was short, and was not full of any great eloquence, it made those residents who were lucky enough to be present proud that they belonged to Lymm. As the train steamed out the party sang "The soldiers' farewell."

div.head: OLD AND WORN-OUT FRUIT TREES.
div.p: OLD AND WORN-OUT FRUIT TREES.

In how many orchards are to be found old decrepit fruit trees that cumber the ground, and are only fit for firewood P When a tree ceases to bear good fruit the wisest and best thing to do with it if its unfruitfulness cannot be improved by top-dressing, the application of liquid manure, removing the exhausted soil and substituting fresh, is to grub it up and replace it with a young, healthy tree. If possible, do not replant in the same station, hut if this cannot be avoided then fresh soil should he added, and every piece of the roots of the, tree which has been removed cleared out so as to guard against fungus attacks.—Wick, in "Farm and Home."

With Uencral Booth as the leader, the Churches of Warrington formed a solid phalanx on Sunday last, the representatives of several denominations taking part in a service alongside each other in the Palace and Hippo- drome.

The Mayor presided, and .those on the plat- form included the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis), the Rev. W. T: Derry, the Rev. Percy meson, Aldermen James Evans, Tinnion, Bennett and J. H. Smethurst, Councillors Lind- ley, Dickenson, Dale, Halliwell and. Henshall, Messrs. C. E. Parker, -W." 'T. Williams, J. Bailey, T. Baxter, and Mrs. James Dodds and Mrs. Tinnion.

The audience was equally varied in its denominational composition. With Colonel ilullary conducting the service, and the Salva- tion Army Band, under Mr. James Lee, leading the singing, the common worship was inspiring. During a speech in praise of the Salvation Army,, the Rector had a word to say upon the variety of religious thought now in association on the platform., "Sometimes," he said, "I may seem to be inconsistent because I do not appear on certain platforms with men for whom I have the deepest respect and the warmest affection. But that is because it is a matter of conscience to me. It may seem a little incon- sistent that I should be here to-day. We find the Mayor everywhere where there is good work being done, and I am with him to-day. The reason why I, who am his chaplain, can- not always go where he goes is because I, un- like him, because of his position, should be compromising • a principle. In attending this meeting, however, there is no question of prin- ciple involved, because the Salvation Army have not for their object the formation of an- other religious body, for, on rescuing people, they encourage them to go back to. that body to which they formerly belonged.

After General Booth's address, Mr. C. B. Parker was called upon to speak, and there developed an interesting incident. Laying a hand with infinite tenderness upon the shoulder of Canon Willis, Mr. Parker remarked: "I am so glad to be on the same Platform as the Rector at a religious meeting, and if his prin- ciples worry him so much that he Cannot come to a Wesleyan meeting, then it is very fortu- nate that wo have 'a Salvation Army meeting where we can come together and unite in wor- ship. (Applause.) I should like more of these meetings, if Only for that purpose, because I love-the Rector as a brother." (Applause.) GENERAL BOOTH AND THE ARMY'S

div.head: MISSIONARIES.
div.p: MISSIONARIES.

The General's address concerned "The Sal- vation Army in -other tand,s,” and he explained that unlike the missionary enterprises of. most denominations the Salvation Army had started its work abroad through the emigration of People who had not gone out specially to be missionaries. In every case excepting China that had been the case. The Army had shown itself to be a movement having life, in itself. It was a movement which had extended itself in the world by the force of its own inli6:ent vitality, its living strength. What started the movement in America was characteristic. A family of silk weavers went to the U.S.A. from Coventry to earn a better living, and once there they resumed the religious meetings, first in their. own homes,- and, when the congrega- tions grew in the course of time, sent for a leader from the London 'headquarters. The work .of the Army was 60 widespread now that it was carried on in some sixty different coun- tries or Colonies, and in some thirty-seven languages, under the direction of 23,000 or 21,000 leaders. The movement started in Hol- land through a Dutch student coming in con- tact with the Army when he was studying' at Paris University. On his return to Amsterdam ' began to hold meetings. (Applause.) Where the Army had gone was not because the leaders had said, "We .will have a Salvation Army here, there, or. elsewhere," but because as members went from place to place in the ordinary way of life. they took the message with -them. . _ •

- During the war the Salvation Army had un- furled its flag in three different countries— Russia, Burmah, and China—and only a 'week or two ago the Chinese Ambassador had told him that the Government had not only given it a good reception, but would do all they could to help it. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the Mayor was passed on the proposition of Mr. C. E. Parker, seconded by. Alderman Tinnion. In the evening the General preached to an- other great "audience assembled in the Hippo- drome.
Before beginning his sermon the General ex- pressed tho hope that an effort would shortly be made to provide the Salvation Army with a new hail in the town.

div.head: HIS LAST LETTER.
div.p: HIS LAST LETTER.
The Rev. H. B. Firth's Parting Message To Parishioners.
HIS IDEALS.

Leaving Warrington at the end of the year to go to Stockport, the Rev. H. B. Firth has penned an interesting letter to his parishioners at 'Latchford. It appears in this month's St. James' Parish Magazine, and is as follows: " It is with a feeling of Sincere regret that I address to you the last Of a long Series of 'Vicar's Letters.' .To lay down the reins of government after a thirteen years' incumbency is no easy matter when one's work has. been happy and congenial, and 1 shall be extremely sorry to leave the parish where I feel I have so many good friends and where the people as a whole have been most kind, helpful and tolerant.

" No one could be more conscious than I am that m 3 ministry "among you has been very iwerfectiy fulfilled; riglitly to preside over, the 'latish, to meke. the Church a Source of inspiration and blessing, to visit and console the sick . and mourners, to Watch over the Young, to keep in touch with all classes of the community,. arc some of the objects that every conscientious parish priest naturally sets before him, :and as one thinks of the great responsi- bility of the pastoral office one can only. say 'who is sufficient for these things,' and pray that God may pardon what has been amiss or neglected. But if the- retrospect is tinged with regret that one's work has not been better accomplished, there is a great deal to make One very thankful that God has vouchsafed many signs of encouragement and tokens of His blessing. The congregation has steadily in- creased and no clergyman could wish , for a more attentive and reverent congregation, to minister to whom has been a privilege and pleasure. Respect for the great Holy Days of the Church has manifested itself in unmistak- able ways, and I Shall ever be thankful for the magnificent response that was made some years ago to make Good . Friday a day of great solemnity and devotion.

div.head: "SOME HAVE DRIFTED AWAY."
div.p: "SOME HAVE DRIFTED AWAY."

"Much of my time, as-you know, has been spent among the. young people of the parish, and the Day -and Sunday Schools, the Bible Classes, the Choir Practices, the Girls' Friendly Society, the Band of Hope, the Confirmation Classes, and the Communicants'. Guilds have afforded 'me frequent opportunities for coming into' contact witli the junior members of the Church. Some, alas, have drifted away into the stream of indifference that. engulfs so many, gut I am happy to think of the splendid body of young men—most of whom. of curse, are now, serving with. the Forces—and women, of boys and girls who are intimately connected with St. James' Parish and its manifold organ- isations. To all those most loyal helpers who have worked and are.still working in different ways for their welfare I am unfeignedly thank- ful.

"Then there has been much to encourage us during the past thirteen years when we reflect on the material progress that has • been achieved. By the kind co-operation of. many helpers our bazaats and sales of work have teen very successful, and by their means and in other ways a large amount of money has been raised and spent with good advantage to the parish; the church has been put into a thoroughly good condition and made most com- fortable and well-equipped for divine. service, a new Mission Church has been built, afid the schools have been repaired and the require- ments of the Board of Education complied with. It, is a Matter .of great satisfaction to me that there is not a single debt connected with any organisation in the parish. There are quite a number of separate funds to be admin, istered, and, without exception, they show a balance on the right side.

Before the war the ancient foot-driven spin- ning wheel had been relegated to the lumber- room, or 'the antique shop, its place being taken by the machinery of the modern mill. Other Examples. The members of the Warrington Caledonian Association, who on St. Andrew's Day dined not only well but wisely, will be ready to repudiate the gross insinuation, but there be those who allege that the one circumstance under which a Scotsman loses his proverbial self-control is when a good dinner is set before him. Still, those who went to the famous anniversary din- ner at Aberdeen in 1806 came back with strange stories of what they • witnessed there. More- over, Mr. Fredk. W..rfockwood, in his amazing compilation entitled "(boil Cheer: The Romance of Food and Feasting," records another of the kind which took place at Edinburgh in 1831. Tt is remembered as "the Ante-benedic- tion Dinner," because the guests did not wait for the customary words of consecration before they fell upon their prey. The fruit was de- voured before the soup was tasted, and even !be presence of Lord Brougham. anti Lord Rose- bery could not set a bridle upon outrageous appetites. The "Annual Register" has a de- tailed description of the scene, but 'enough of -this. Christmas Cheer.

The article on" Christmas Shopping" set me thinking of Christmas feasting. At this season our ancestors, would eat peacocks, swans, and monster pies, to say nothing of plum porridge, the origin of the Christmas pudding of which " Tommy " and " Jack " are to have a share, along with the rest of us—thanks to generous Warrington and other contributors. In 1765 from Northumberland, long famous for its Christmas pies, a pie was despatched which took two men to carry it to the table It was com- posed of two bushel* of flour, twenty pounds of butter, four geese, two turkeys, two rabbits, four wild ducks, two woodcocks, six snipes, four part- ridges, two neat's tongues, two curlews, seven blackbirds, and six pigeons. In. the 26th of Henry 111., an order was given to the Sheriff of Gloucester to send to the King twenty salmon to be put into Christmas pies, and to the Sheriff of Suffolk ten brawns, ten peacocks, ,and other items for the same Purpose. Now, with- out being a bigoted upholder of the cheese diet; or of the no-starch movement, or of .the anti- cookery crusade, or a nut-food fiend, I am a food-reformer to the .extent of rejoicing that those "good old times" are right away in the bygones, and that our dietetic habits .have so improved that We can listen with sympathy, as well as equanimity to the counsels of those who strongly urge us to be abstemious and reason- able during the coming Christmas festivities in especial. At all events I know of some who will not go to excess this Christmas—those who are or are destined soon to be in gaol. A chaplain used to tell how on several occasions he had on Christmas morning conducted Divine service at military prisons, or,' as they are now called detention barracks, or, as " Tommy " himself calls them,, "clink.". The rev, gentleman con- fessed that he greatly disliked preaching to the detained ones. What could he say to them? To wish a happy. Christmas and many*returns. of the day might seem like mockery. The consola- tion ho gave generally took some such form as this: " You, dear brethren, whose liberty is re-; stricted, may pity yourselves to-day, but to- morrow you will wake up with clear, cool heads, with eyes their natural colour, and the satisfac- tion of feeling that you have not to take up any of the time of police courts, which is all too short for the' work to be done in them at this ` happy ' season." However, it's all going to be so different this ,time.
