IN THE COURTS.
THEFT OF OATS.
Carter And Coal Dealer Heavily
Fined.

At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, Peter Regan, 17, Hoyle-street, carter, was charged with the larceny of three bags of oats, valued at £3 155., the property of the Cheshire Lines Committee, and Thos. Hughes, 5, Beard-street, coal dealer, was charged with receiving same, knowing them to be stolen.

Mr. Iv: S. Steel appeared for the Cheshire Lines Committee, Mr. C. IL Unsworth repre- sented Regan, and Mr. F. H. Swallow appeaeed for Hughes. Having consulted with their re- spective solicitors, both defendants pleaded guilty. Mr. Steel said the defendants had known each other for several years. Quite recently Messrs. Gartone, Ltd., had got from Manches- ter 500 sacks of oats, and the defendant Regan was engaged in carrying them from the railway station to the warehouse. Various complaints had been received as to shortage, and as a re- sult of inquiries 'made by Detective Cuthbert, of the company's staff, and Detectives Red- dington. and Anderson, of .the Warrington Police Force, they interviewed Regan. At first he denied all knowledge of any sacks of Oats, but afterwards admitted that on one occasion he had a bag too Many and put it into a hotel yard in Winwick-street. He was taking the bag back when he met Mr. Hughes and sold it to him. He told him about another sack in the hotel yard and Mr. Hughes came and took it away. The detectives subsequently traced one full sack and two empty ones, and when Hughes was charged with receiving, he said: "I did receive it, not knowing it to be stolen, and I gave ss. for the sack." The value of the sucks was 255. each. Mr. Steel explained the position in which the company was placed owing to shortage of labour, and while admit- ting that there were temptations in the way of men like Regan handling large masses of goods, if there were no, such men as Hughes they would not be inclined to steal.

div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
Owners' Responsibility For
Untrained Horses.

A yak important case to cyclists has, just been settled in the King's Bench, and clears up a point which has been in dispute for many years. The facts were that a nurse was riding bicycle along a road near Tonbury one even- ing last January. She had a lamp on her bicycle and it was burning properly. The de- fendant, a farmer, had wished to transfer a colt, an unbroken animal about 18 months old, from one farm to another, and was bringing the colt along the road. In front he had a boy leading a mare; then came the colt following the mare; and behind the colt the defendant himself was driving a .trap to keep the colt from bolting back. When the •plaintiff approached the colt was startled by the light on her bicycle and darted from one side of ,the road to the other, and knocked the plaintiff over, causing injuries for which she sued in this action. The County Court Judge found that the defendant had been negligent, and gave 'judgment for the plaintiff. The case then went .to appeal, and was tried before Mr. Justice Lush and Mr. ,Justico Bail- hache, who upheld tho CoUntr Court Judge's opinion and confirmed the judgment in favour of the cyclist. ,In .the course pf his judgment Mr. Justice Lush put the whole position regard- ing straying animals very clearly, and I cannot do better than quote his actual decision: " The mere fact," be stated, " that a domestic animal strayed on a highway and caused damage there did not necessarily make its owner liable. But the animal in this case was One which was likely to do harm, and which everyone must have known. was likely to do so. Even if there had been no evidence of that—as there was—the Judge would have been justi- fied in taking notice of it and of the fact' that this sort of accident was likely to happen. Assuming that the natural propensity of the animal was—as it clearly was—to do this sort of of thing, there was, in his opinion, a clear breach of duty by the defendant. If a person placed on a highway an animal likely in cer- tain circumstances to •Pdo .harm be • must take• reasonable precautions to prevent it from doing. harm. An unbrolien colt on a dark night, not' under control, was likely to do exactly what this one did. It caused the damage not by doing some mischief its tendency to which was unknown, but by doing just what in the cir- cumstances it might have been expected to do." Perhaps the result of this decision will, bd. to make owners of horses a little more careful than they are particularly in out-Of-the-way districts. THE SIDESLIP DANGER.

Even the most careful motOr-eyClist is. liable when the roads are greasy to have. a sideslip. It is when the roads are greasy that the great- est difficulty arises.. ,Wet roads are not nearly so dangerous as .are . those which are midway between The wet and dry stages. It is under these conditions that the motor-cyclist must exercise, the greatest Care. The dangers of greasy roads can, to a largo extent, be overcome by following a. few simple rules. CHAPTER XXVIII.

ON THE WINGS OF THE MORNING. In a dream sat Arthur Stanleigh. Blair, a thief —rich on the plutider from the oil wells and mines —and Vivian was his wife, had been for months! The double revelation crushed the young man. He would drink a toast to death and end it all. Plac- ing before him the baleful jewel, he prepared a poisoned glass of brandy and stood to drink it, when the curtains parted and into the room walked 'Luke Lovell. Straight to the table he went, and snatched the diamond. Strange irony of fate. The gem desired, the great jewel that from "at charm against harm" had come to, be a curse, was grasped again by Luke's gipsy hands that, strong as they were, were never to hold it. John Powell, some time Arthur Stanleigh ot Stan- leigh Hall. son of Hagar Harding, sat collapsed in his chair. As Luke Lovell seized the diamond the prayer of Hagar Harding fluttered to the' table. Luke growled and tore it from Arthur's resisting grasp, glanced at it, and tossed it back in scorn. "You live soft," he sneered "Live soft in your luxury, while I have wandered like a hunted wolf in the wilds. But now' shall live soft, and you shall be my servant and my banker." As in a, daze, Arthur sat relaxed, without 'hope and without fear. Yes, he had reached the end of everything. The prayer of his mother had come home as a curse in this hour of.„.his shame and humiliation. He had been the sorrow and sacrifice of her young motherhood and the heartbreak of her maturity. Esther, whom he had despoiled of birthright and patrimony, her steadfast faith outraged at last, had left him in scorn and contempt. Blair, for whose sake he had borne undessrvedly the brand of Cain, and by his flight from Virginia had accepted the onus of Blair's guilt for the murder of Dr. Lee— Blair, too, had been false and faithless to every trust. Vivian? The scales had dropped from his eyes. She, too, was false. Without fear and without hope! Crushed and dazed, the so-called John Powell gazed at the poisoned glass of brandy with which he had stood to pledge a toast to death when Luke had burst in upon him. Then his eyes turned upon Luke. "I look strange to you, huh?" said Luke, answer- ing the look. "They shaved me and they clipped me in the pen, where you and Blair Stanleigh sent me. The express slip was all the proof that was needed against the poor, ignorant gipsy. They shut me up like a rat in a trap from the light and air in a rotten prison for stealing money that you stole, the money from the train robbers. I went back over all our tracks and found the dead horse, also the empty cache. There were clues plain enough when I got out of prison and went back. That stolen money you found in the desert was the start of your fortune, Mr. John Powell.' The money was secretly repaid by you, but when they caught one of the poor robbers—as they thought—in me, they sent me to the pen. "I don't look like I used to, do I? That's prison pallor that even the sun of the desert couldn't wholly take away. I'm thinner, too, but I'll fatten on you. I'll spare your life hecau;-i you are Hagar's son, but if I go to prison you will go with me, for I have the proofs that you found and used the stolen money, and I know you left Virginia as Arthur Stanleigh, accused of murder! " Where is your so-called cousin, your pal and fellow crook, Blair Stanleigh? Out with the fair lady, I suppose? He shall feed and clothe me and be my banker, too. Durand, who helped you to send me to prison is dead. I hear. All fine gentle- men, the whole of you, eh? Well, I shall be a gentleman, too, a regular Romany Rye. You know what that means—lt means gipsy gentleman. And now that I have fed, come and clothe me. You shall be my flunkey. One Romany Rye as valet to another." Luke rose from where he had gorged, and Arthur followed him without a word to his suite of rooms and wardrobe upstairs. . .
While Luke Lovell was in Arthur's rooms dress-
ing himself in the young man's clothes, putting on his jewellery and taking his money, Blair and Vivian were sheltering from the rain in a wayside restaurant. To the same resort came a young man
- - and woman--Dick Jones and a friend whom he called

" Gert." At the sight of Blair Stanleigh Mr. Joned was somewhat abashed. But some recollection came to him that steadied him, and he greeted Blair with an assumed indifference. Blair gave the new- comers a surly, supercilious stare. "Who are they?" asked Vivian. • I don't know the blonde female with him," re- plied Blair, carelessly; "but the boozy gentleman is Dick Jones, who was our shipping clerk at the Fair Hope Oil Company offices—until I fired him for coming to work after being out the night before as you see him now." " You didn't fire yourself for that offence, or John Powell, the boss, I assume?" remarked Vivian, sarcastically. "No matter what I do the night before, my head is clear and my hands steady next day," Blair answered. "As for John Powell—`my boss,' as you call him—since he has taken to drugs and flying machines we do not see him at the office. That reminds me. I am sick of the whole business. I have got the money in my own name. I am tired of hanging on like a parasite till he drugs himself to death. When do we get away?" _

"When we get The Diamond from the Sky," re- plied Vivian. "I have set my heart and soul on having it. It must turn up again." At the other table Jones was chaffing his, com- panion. Toying with a fake jewel the woman was. wearing, 'Jones said "Pretty nifty, Gert; but it's not a patch on the diamond which came by ex- press to John Powell. It was worth a million. I was sent to the house with it. He opened the packet and nearly had a fit, for there inside was a case and in that case was a letter that stung him hard, and with it was a chain and locket about a thousand years old. And in that locket was a diamond as big as a walnut. I think it was the same diamond that the circus proprietor .gave the

lady lion-tamer. Then the lion killed the lady, and her husband the clown killed the proprietor and then shot himself. Remember? John Powell bought the diamond at the auction of the busted circus, then someone stole it from him', and John Powell got it back by express, just as I'm telling you. He gave me fifty dollars to keep my mouth shut about it. But I don't have to keep my mouth shut about anything for anybody, for all I got for the way I worked in his office was to be thrown out. Wait till I see Powell; I'll get my job back all right, and nobody will stop me." Blair and Vivian had sat tv- -- though electrified at the fiist words they overheard about the diamond. When the tipsy clerk had ceased speaking Blair stood beside him.
"You'll get your job back all right. Jones," he said, hoarsely. "Here's fifty dollars from me. Tell me again about the diamond coming by express."
The- clerk repeated his story. Even while he was .speaking Vivian had called the waiter to bring the bill and their wraps. Once ,in their great roadster Blair put on fill speed.

"The cunning bOundef," cried he. "Arthur has had the diamond safe and sound and hidden from us right under our very noses for six months." "How shall; wq get it.?" asked Vivian, eagerly. "Leave that to Me," 'said ,Blair,- fiercely. "The: time is ripe. We've got his money; Durand is dead; De Vaux was evidently paid his price and sent the diamond back. He has skipped far away, and need not be reckoned with. John Powell is no good to himself or anyone else; he is better dead. When he is dead I can tell you who he really is, and the Earldom in England will be mine. You will be a peeress, Vi." Get me The Diamond from the Sky first," an- swered Vivian.

"There won't be any trouble about that," re- marked Blair. "The diamond is hidden in the house, and we will find it after Arthur Stanleigh alias John Powell is dead." As he spoke he stopped the machine, for they had, reached the aviation field and the hangar where John Powell, amateur airman, kept his latest toy, his aeroplane. Blair took a tyre-iron from the tool- box, wrenched the hasp from the door and entered the hangar. A file was on the work-bench. Just a
little tampering with the stay-brace wires, but sufficient. The next time John Powell took a flight Death would ride beside him.

Vivian asked no questions. She understood and shuddered. For the man who was to die had been in her arms, and her caresses had beguiled him. But she must choose, and as between the masterful Blair and the weakling doomed to die there was but one choice—for with Arthur Stanleigh dead and Blair Stanleigh come into his heritage, all would be hers, she knew.

Well dressed, with a pocket-book well lined with notes, Luke Lovell went downstairs, followed by Arthur Stanleigh, who weakly sank into a chair. "You haven't seen the last of me, mind," sneered Luke. "But before I go I'll drink you very good health." And Luke seized the poisoned glass of brandy and drank it. "Oh, you villain, you have done me!" shrieked the man in agony as the deadly liquid did its work. Staggering out of the house into the road, he fell prone just as the car driven by Blair came down the road and ran over him.

"It is Arthur," whispered Blair, "disfigured be- yond recognition." "Are you certain?" asked the girl. "Yes,. see, here is his pocket-book and, oh heavens, The Diamond from the Sky!" Both realised that no further scheming would be required. Unnecessary was the filing of the wire stay. Another crime would not stain their hands. After many trials and much tribulation—the road to possession of the diamond had been rough, very rough—the great gem was theirs, and with Arthur's 'money and the wealth that would be theirs with the titles of Earl and Countess, the course through life would be rosy. Vivian would realise her ambi- tion to' wear The Diamond from the Sky, a lady with the best of them.

During the journey westward Hagar had been slowly dying. Nothing but her deep love for Esther and her strong faith that she could reach her son in time to save him had held Hagar to life. A harvest of heartaches, through the yeats of sor- row and sacrifice had sapped her spirit and her physical strength. Only a sweet complacent faith had sustained her. Now' the shock of a lightning stroke, the burning of the van, and the exposure to the storm had hastened her passing. Esther despatched Quabba to Los Angeles to bring back Arthur. "Let nothing prevent you see- inV him. Tell him that his mother is dying and he must come." Quabba did not find Arthur in Los Angeles. Instead, he read of his death—killed by a motor car driven by Blair Stanleigh! As quickly as he could the gipsy rode back to the caravan.

- Arthur Stanleigh, however, was not dead. He watched Luke stagger into the road, saw the motor- car strike him, and from the actions of Blair and Vivian, realised that they believed he lay dead before them. Half-demented he said, "I will fly to Esther on the wings of the morning," and going to the hangar left for the plains in his aeroplane. In their camp a few miles from Los Angeles the gipeies watched the great, bird in the sky coming towards them. Steadily the machine came along and then slowly dipped towards them. Suddenly the bird fiutteied strangely. Blair's murderous treachery did its work; a wire snapped, and the machine crashed to the ground a heap of twisted metal.

With cries of dismay the gipsies ran to the wrecked aeroplane, with them Esther. She, too, had seen the bird out of the west, and wondered if at last Arthur had repented and was coming to make peace with his sorely-tried mother. Out of the wreckage the gipsies raised the uncon- scious man tenderly. "It is Arthur," cried Esther in distress. "Is he dead?" Applying ready methods to the faintly breathing form, the gipsies won him- back to consciousness. (To be continued.)

"No, ma'am; the machine stops all right, but I and My fare always keep on going ahead, mostly in the air. Must go some- where, you know, ma'am!".

(Lancashire Section.)
BEST OF THE •SEASON.
le Game With Wigan Al Wilders- poOl.

This match was looked forward to with great interest by the enthusiasts of Wilderspool. As with all previous matches between these old rivals, the players went at it hammer and tongs, giving no quarter nor asking any, with the result that those who took the trouble to wend their way to Wilderspool were amply repaid, as the game was birufar the best we have seen this season.

. As in the previous home match,: the Feather had just enough bite in it to make the players move. The teams set to work. immediately, and Warrington—through that redoubtable six— were very soon tapping the -Wigan defence to see if there were any short cuts- over the "coveted rut," and they were quickly re- warded, for within five minutes from the kick- off the home team were three ,points up as the result of one of -those familiar forward rushes Which swept the opposition aside like brush- wood.

This acted as a tonic upon the visitors, for no sooner had the game been recommenced than they took the lead. A Well-judged, long- swinging pass by Johnny Thomas put Bradley in possession, and, making straight for the corner, safely planted the ball there, for Jolley to convert with a well-directed kick from an acute angle. And so it was right throughout, the score fluctuating every five or ten minutes, and thus making the contest interesting to the end.

Play moved with dazzling rapidity—just the sort the spectators ,enjoy. The passing of the visitors was, at times, brilliant, and in striking contrast to that of the home backs. Many of Wigan's movements reminded one of the days before the War, in the manner in which they flung the ball about and in the general under- standing that existed in the team, not the least feat Ore being in the way they covered one another.

As we have said, Warrington were slovenly; the passing was ill-tithed, there were poor finishing touches, and a general lack of method; and had it net been for the forwards the game would never have ended in victory.

With the exception of Jolley, none of the other backs covered themselves • with glory. By the way, it was interesting to watch these. two, brothers trying to outwit each other, but the honours were even throughout. Of course, the three quarters certpinly did their share in some very fine defence, but, as one has said many times before, a lot of defending is the result of not being able to set up an attack. In this department none did better than Jolley, Tranter, Dainteth and Brookes, the latter looking well after Bradley after, the surprise move early in the game, and taking care that it was not repeated.

What a glorious chance it, was Brookes had in the second half; no one to beat and half the field to cover; but he was crying bellows- to-mend long before he got there, so no one was surprised when he did not pull it off.

The half-backs were weak, lacking initiative, and one would rather see young Jones playing stand-off. Too much praise cannot be showered upon the vanguard, for they were the life and soul of the team. To a man the forwards acquitted themselves well and gave the hefty six opposed to them a gruelling time. Without a doubt they are the finest six in Lancashire at the present time., One cannot say more than that.

div.head: MATCH IN DETAIL.
div.p: THE MATCH IN DETAIL.

Fog was settling over the Warrington ground when Wigan, the visitors, won the toss, a cir- cumstance which brought them no advantage. B. Jolley, the home back,. missed the ball badly, but recovered finely, and Horrocks and Potter getting possession rushed towards the Wigan line, which was crossed by Jones five minutes from the start. Jolley failed to add the goal. Tranter mulled near the Warrington goal, but the ball was got safely away. Brad- ley looked getting through for Wigan, but an infringement robbed him of a fine chance. A moment later the same player, rushed over with a fine try and J. Jolley added the goal. Warrington maintained a steady pressure and B. Jolley, getting into a good position, dropped for goal and succeeded in gathering ih another couple of points. Only a few minutes had elapsed when the Wigan Jolley took a drop at goal and succeeded in lowering the home colours. B. Jolley stopped an ugly rush by Wigan, -who were pressing somewhat heavily, and Potter and Horrocks cleverly car- ried the war into the Wigan quarters. Just on half-time B. Jolley was heavily charged and had to be attended to. Half-time:— Wigan, 2 goals I try (7 points); Warrington, 1 goal 1 try t 5 points). At the beginning of the second half Jones, the Warrington forward, dribbled nearly half the length of the field and some exciting play took place under the Wigan posts. Thomas got the ball away, but Potter and Dainteth re- turned it again, and the home players experi- enced hard lines in not scoring. The danger was, however, cleared with a penalty kick. Warrington, who *ere playing a strong game, came again, and only a resolute defence kept them in check. Wigan continued on the de-1 fence and Tranter made a great effort to put his ' side ahead, but J. Jolley tackled him finely At last tilt efforts of the home team were rewarded,' for, from "a penalty _kick, B. Jolley equalised the scores to the ,delight of the home crowd. 'Not to be denied, .Warrington came again, and after some exciting play Brookes received possession, and, beating all opposition, he went over at the Corner for a grand try. B. Jolley, with a brilliant goal, put his side five points ahead. The kick-oirt had no sooner been effected than Brookes received at mid- field and raced away half the length of the field,. but he was not fast enough to get through. Warrington continued in an aggres- sive mood and Wigan were given a rare gruel- ling. Warrington pressed to the end. Final :-- Warrington, 3 goals 2 tries (12 points); Wigan, 2 goals 1 try (7 points). • The teams were ' Warrington: 13. Jolley; Brookes, Tranter, Potter: Horrocks; Dainteth, Jones; Harmer, Green, Cunliffe, Matthews, Dumbell, J. Jones. ' Wigan': J. Jolley; Bradley, Sherrington, Heaton, Smith; Hesketh, Thomas; Francis, H. Bankes, Melling, Whalley, Blackledge, Magraw. Referee,. Mr. F. Ratcliffe, Swinton.

div.p: Town's 111-Luck At Altrincham.

O 1 excellent quality was tilt football witnessed at Altrincham an Saturday, when 'Warrington Town played the return game, and the few spec- tators• -were provided with many incidents which aroused enthusiasm. Ihe first half did not pro- duce a goal.- The best farward play of the match was provided by Aspinall and Woodhouse, the latter supplying his partner with many delight- ful and beautifully judged passes, which should have enabled the centre-forward to put the ball into the net on at least two occasions- But Altrincham paid marked attention to these two, and tackled vigorously and strongly. Just as Aspinall. threatened to lead a raid, Johnson lunged the ball up the field. Banner was about to return it when Siddall bore down upon him, and taking the ball with. him. snot ,with great force. Kite fell full length and Made a brilliant save at-the expense of a corner, from which the Altrincham centre-forward headed over the .bar. A brilliant effort by Siddall for the Town met with ill-luck, the ball ,hitting the cross-bar. Woodhouse, from twenty yards range, met the rebound, and once more the luck was against the Town, the ball again hitting the cross-bar. Eric% side was having a fair share of the play, and several shots from each team hit the .cross- bar. •

Warrington were without two of their regular players, Millward and Stephens, both of whom were on the sick list. Connor, who the, previous week played so well foil Altrincham, when they, were short. of:a prayer, was given a trial, and had the misfortune to. be placed out of action three times, with the result that he was little more than a. passenger. Banner, the left winger, had to go .full-back, and Siddali right half. Kite in goal did not field so perfectly as usual, and early in the first half let the ball rebound from him at great risk. That may ,have disturbed
'Ls equanimity, but the fact remains _that he
never seemed -sure, and it was generally at a second time:that he gathered: the ball. The full-backs, especially Leah, played well. Banner,

however, is out of place at fiill--back. The Town half-backs were the better set, and the man, above, all-- others, stupendous :and scorning fatigue, waM,eorge Whitfield, while Siddall at- tained his usual high standard. The, Warring- ton, forwards never got into their swing. Toward S the end of the game fog completely smothered the ground, and eight' minutes from time Siddalt- scored for Altrincham, but a min-
.e later Aspinall equalised in brilliant fashion.

Before the close, however, the home team got another, by which they were victorious. Result: Altrincham, 2 goals; Warrington Town, 1 goal. div.head: JUNIOR NOTES.
div.p: JUNIOR NOTES.

A very even and keenly contested game was! witnessed on the Steel-street ground last week, when Appleton Hornets were the visitors. At ' the interval the score 'was one goal to nil in favour of the Saints, and in the second portion the Saints added a couple ,of goals and the Hornets ,scored from a penalty kick. On the general run of the game the visitors ,had their share of the play, and on many occasions their, forwards showed fine combination, but when near goal they weie met by a pair of good backs in Furness and Tunstall. Whatever shots came in Povey's way they were dealt with satisfac- torily, and in the middle lipe Miller was the most conspicuous.

Hare made his first appearance at centre-for- ' ward, and gav4 a Creditable display, and Boyle ha S rejoined his old club and taken up the out- side right position, and gave satisfaction. In the ,visitors' ranks Pegg came in as goalkeeper in a case of emergency, and did very well. Thornton and Fozard kicked strongly and tvell. The half-backs were inclined to be weak, and the forwards were about equal and gave a better display of combination movements than the Saints' front line.

Widnes St. Mary's appeared in the Park in opposition to the Latchford Recs., but,were un- able to repeat their performance of the previous week, and at the close of play they had to acknowledge defeat by the odd goal in three.

The Grappenhall lads were the surprise packet of the League. They travelled to the Tanhouse- lane ground, and after a good hard and clean game, Succeeded in defeating the home team by two goals against one. But xiuring the game
one unsatisfactory incident occurred, hnd that was that the Grappenhall backs, under. heavy. pressure, put the half between their own goal- posts. This time Rigby was the offender.

The, Howley United and the cadets played their return fixture in the Park., which resulted in an easy win for the United by four deaf goals. For two or three weeics in succession the UnitA have not beeir able to put their best team in the field for various reasons. In this fixture they commenced with only eight Players, and the Cadets were slightly tne better 'team until the late comers turned out, after which play was mostly in favour of the United.
Miller, ;the Cadets' custodian, gave a fine dis- Lay, and was chiefly responsible for saving, his LS team from a heavier defeat.
Lunt and Massey also played. well, and Daven- port at ceatre-for ward was ndt well supported by his colleagues. •

For the United .Walters was not very seriously troubled during the match. Foster, although he commenced in erratic form, gave .pne of his best displays.- Miller had- mita to do in breaking up the Cadets' attacks.
_Rutter, who is a new player to.the.United,.is showing good form, and with more exporietic, he will be worth ,his place. Hassan,. Hnmphries and Gleave were the pick of the forwards.

Hubbersty is proving a good find for the-Rees. There should be a very keen game on the County ground. . The Hornets should now be able to add points to their total, as most of their matches are at Page-lane.

St. Mary's: Mercer; Gahan, Atherton; Clare, Cooper, Bennett; White, Fairclough, McAlister, Gregory and Crewe. Referee, Mr. S. C. Essenhigh.. A very fast pace was set, Gregory showing up well on the visitors' left. Green then set the home forwards going and a rush was made on the Saints' goal, but the home forwards were checked by the Off-side rule. The game now turned in. favour of the visitots. They attacked the home goal very keenly, and were unfortun- ate in not opening their score. A strong-appeal was made by the visitors, but the referee ruled

that the ball had been over the line in mid air. Half-time: No goals. The second half opened in favour of the visit- ors, and a strong attack on the Recs.' goal re- sulted in several corner kicks being conceded by the home defence without any result to. the visitors. Play was gradually transferred to the Saints' end, and after Mercer had successfully dealt with several good shots he had to sur- render his charge to a fine shot by Heasom. From the centre kick the Recs. attacked again, but were quickly put on the retreat by Gahan and Atherton. By good combination the Recs.' goal was again the scene of action, and Bennett was successful in making the scores•equal. After this some keen play was witnessed in the at- tempt to gain the lead, and each defence was hard pressed to clear their lines. The home forwards adopted the kick-and-rush policy,, and raced towards the Saints' goal, and James gained the lead for the BRCS. From now to, the call of time the visitors showed the better. form,. but
failed to add to their score, the final result being: Latchford Recs., 2' goarsi. Widlies. St. Mary's, 1 goal.

A keen attack was now, made on the Saints' goal, and Furness had to- concede a 'corner kick. This 'proved fruitless,;nand the. game was more keenly fought, each end being , visited in quick succession, but the respective defenders cleared their lines. Another attack by the Saints saw, Tegg leave his goal and clear in fine style, and a little later the Saints had a goal disallowed, the referee's whistle going before the ball passed between the posts. After a. long spell of even play in midfield the home team again got in touch with the visitors' backs, and Boyle scored from a mehs\e in front of goal. Still keeping_ up the pressure, Miller continued to give a good display, but after twenty minutes' play Humphries scored from a well,plaeed corner by. Hibbert. From the centre kick the United again attacked the Cadets' goal, and ,Gleave put them further ahead with a very fine effort. The Cadets now played more keenlY, and Davenport led an attack on the Howley goal. Walters brought off -a smart clearance when the movement looked very dangerous. Half-time: Howley United, 2 goals; Latchford Cadets, nil. The United quickly showed the better form on resuming, and were seen to better' advan- tage than their opponents. For a while the Cadets staved off all 'attacks, but eventually they had to yield to a petialty kick, from which Miller scored the third goal. After this reverse the Cadets played more strenuously, and on several occasions the United defence had to exert Themselves to keep their goal ' intact. Foster defended strongly and kieked finely. Cheques Handed Over At Smoking Concert.

Over one hundred members of the Warrington and District Amateur Bowling Association were present in the Assembly Room of the Lion. Hotel on Saturday evening, when prizes to suc- cessful bowling teams, and cheques to local charitable institutions were presented. A tea was enjoyed in the afternoon, over which Mr. F. Dean (chairman of the Council) pre- sided. 4r. W. P. Rylands took the chair at the evening gathering, and amongst others pres- ent were: The Mayor (Alderman Peacock), Mr. T. Garnett (vice-chairman of the Council), Mr. G. F. Freeman (hon. treasurer), Mr. J. Wood (hon. secretary), and Messrs. T. Brookes Hand- ley (representing the Thelwall Heys Military Convalescent Home), Mr. A. Bottomley (White- cross Auxiliary Hospital), Mr. J. H. J. Ramp- son (secretary of the Infirmary), Mr. George Walker (Working Men's Infirmary Committee), and Mr. Harry Hope (Warrington and District Nursing Association). The Chairman said Warrington men were fond of cricket and football, but bowling was their 'game. A man needed the finest qualities he ,could possess to be a good bowler—courage, de- termination, good temper, and patience. Bowlers were always in the forefront of anything which made for good; just as they were with regard to the local charities. As the result of the generosity and public spirit of Mr. W. Green, who some time ago brought a team of profes- sional bowlers to play against a picked team of Warrington amateurs—a most notable incident, and the first event of the kind in Warrington. for a considerable number of years—a sum of £43 was raised, which was to be distributed that night. (Applause.)

div.head: TIIE APPORTIONMENT.
div.p: TIIE APPORTIONMENT.

The Chairinan then presented cheques to the following institutions :—Warrington Infirmary, £10; Wnitecross Auxiliary Hospital, Al; Had- don Court Hospital, Al; Thelwall Heys Mili- tary Convalescent Hospital, £7; "The Ex- aminer" Army Christmas Padding Fund for .Soldiers, £5; Oaklands Auxiliary Hospital, ) aresbury, ; Warrington District Nursing Association, £2; Warrington Children's Summer Camp, .12.. Mr. Hampson said that owing to the increased cost of provisions the Infirmary badly needed financial assistance. He was afraid there would be .a deficit at the end of the year. Mr. Bottomley said there was accommodation at the Whiteeross Hospital for 310 patients, and preparations were being made for two hundred more beds. More than one thousand soldiers who had been nursed at the hospital had all ex- pressed themselves quite satisfied with the treat- ment received.
Mr. Handley remarked that of .21,500 needed each year for the unkeep of the Thelwall Heys Hospital, the Government provided only .2800 or £9OO.

The Mayor received the cheque for the Christ- mas Pudding Fund, and said that everything which ,we did for the "boys" who were so nobly fighting our battles was well deserved. A letter from Sir Arthur Pearson, on behalf of the Blinded Soldiers' and Sailors' Hostel, St. Dun Stan's, Regent's Pail, London, was read, acknowledging .210 from the Association. Mr. Hope replied on behalf of the Nursing Association.

The championship prizes were then presented as follows: Crosfield Challenge Cup and cheque, Senior Conservative team;' runners-up, cheque, - Junior Conservatives; consolation winners, :• .Rylands's No. 1 team, cheque; runners-up, Bank Quay Bowling Club, cheque. - On behalf of the Bank Quay team, Mr. A. (Applause.) Mr. Hope proposed a Vote of thanks to the Chairman, who, in responding, proposed the health of the Hon. Secretary (Mr. Wood) and Mr. W. Green, to whom, he said, the receipt a the- £4.3 was practically due. Mr. W. Patrick proposed the health of the s' Mayor. \A musical programme was given during the evening. Messrs. T. ANOTHER PROTEST.

div.head: To the Editor of "The Examiner."
div.p: To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—l have waited for some one more able to witite on the above matter so far as the Labour section are. concerned. As no one has, so far, taken the .subject in .hand, I feel compelled to Protest against the Labour men being left out in this matter.

• While not 'objecting to the names placed on the Bench, it is only just and right that some one from the Labeur group should have a seat as J.P. 'At the, present time we have not a single magistrate in Warrington that can. be called a Labour magistrate. Other towns, and even small ones, can have Labour representation on the 'Judicial Bench. Why not 'Warrington? Are we in Warrington so far advanced that we do not require any? Or is it that we do not want any? I think the whole Labour men in the town. should take this up and send a.strong protest to the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lan- caster; and so try to get some Labour represen- tatives in this town.

I feel, as Mr. Maginn feels, that each section in the town should be fully recognised. We. are expected to do our share in other things. Why not in this?, Or is Someone keeping us out politically? I therefore ask you to allow me to add our strong protest 'and trust others ,will do the same till Labour is fully allowed its fair share in all local affairs. Thanking you in allowing me space.
I remain,"yours truly, FREDERICK HODSON. National Union of Dock LabourerS and Riverside Workers, 121 a, Sankey-street.
HONOUR TO FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
Mr. T. P. Bradshaw Congratulated
Upon His Appointment.

There was an enthusiastic meeting of the "Prince of Wales" Lodge of OddfellowS on Saturday evening, when P.P.G.31. 'Thomas P. •Bradshaw was congratulated on his appoint- ment as a magistrate for the borough. N.G.W. Hill presided. P.P.G,M. H. Lawrence, in moving the resolu- tion, said that they knew of the great work Bro. Bradshaw had done for Oddfellowship in the Warrington district, and, in fact, for Friendly Society work generally. He was well deserving of the honour that had been Con- ferred upon him, and they desired, as a Lodge, to offer him their congratulations: (Applause.) Bro: Bradshaw had been actively engaged in Friendly Society work for several years .and he had not spared himself when anything could be done •to help forward the work .of .oddfellowship.. Although,they.naturally looked upon the appointment as an honour to their Lodge, they also realised that, in view of the work- that Bro. -Bradshaw had done, it was really. an 'honour to all Friendly Societies in Warrington.' The Other. societies in the town realised this, as was shown by the letters of 'congratulation received from them. (Hear, hear.) , ir Arthur Crosfield and Mr. Bradsha,.v's Fine Record.

Sir Arthur Crosfield, an hororary member of the society,, wrote to Bro. Bradshaw, and after referring to his splendid and honourable record of work for the great benefit of his fellow- townsmen. he said :—" What you have achieved in this really fine record of unselfish. high- minded and -noble work is familiar to all your fellow-townsmen; and therefore. nO more 'popu- lar .and no better-deserved appointment to the Bench could possibly have been Made. , I warmly and heartily congratUlatEi you, and I no less sincerely congratulate the magistrates on that Bench, knowing, as I. do full Well, the efficiency and experience, high character and capacity and dignity with which your duties will, be discharged. May I say, in conclusion, as an old Member of more than one Friendly Society, I rejoice in the honour paid to those societies in .your appointment." (Applause.) Bro. Lawrence, in conclusion, said. they all hoped that Bro. 'Bradshaw would be given health and long life to carry out his important duties, and he moved :—" That this Lodge de- sires to express its sincere appreciation of the high honour conferred upon pne of its Members in the 'person of P.P.G.M. Thos. P. Bradshaw, who has recently been placed on the Commis- sion of the Peace for the County Borough of .Warrington,, and offers him its heartiest con- gratulations on the appointment. The mem- bers also desire to record their appreciation of the services willingly and unselfishly rendered by Bra. Bradshaw to Oddfellowship in particu- lar and to Friendly Society work in general, and to express the pleasure it has given them to know that his services have .been recognised In..such".a. signal and deserving manner."
P.G. Thomas Reddish seeoii-ded the-proposi- tion and eulogised the work that Bro. Brad- shaw had done for the Lodge. The honouli was well merited.
P.P.G.M. IL H. Radford and the N.G. sup- ported the resolution. A Common-sense Magistrate.

'P.P.G.A.T. T. S. Steel, as a :trustee of the oldest Lodge in the town and as .a Past Officer' of the District; supported the resolution. .Jie could -assure them that the honour conferred on Bro. Bradshaw was appreciated. by all, Odd- fellows in Warrington. From his long ac- quaintance with Bro. Bradshaw, he was confi- dent that he would` bring to bear upon the discharge of his duties as a magistrate good, sound common-sense and a knowledge of human nature, and. that be would prove an acquisition to the Bench. (Applause.) The resolution having been passed with acclamation, .P.P.G.M. Bradshaw said he re- garded the appointment. as an honour to Friendly Societies and as a reward for the work he had tried to do for Oddfellowship. He looked back with pleasure on his convection with that Lodge, and they might rely on a, continuance of his interest in Friendly Society work. With regard to his duties as a magis- trate, he should discharge them to the best of his ability and without fear or favour. He was glad that the appointment had met with. the approval'of his brethren, and Ile thanked them for the resolution of Congratulations they had passed. • The Mayor Congratulated.

A resolution of congyatula,tion was also passed to Bro. Peter Peacock, the Mayor, who is an honorary member of the Lodge, on his appointment as A Justice of the Peace, ' and the Secretary,was instructed to convey the best wishes of the members to the Mayor.
